Family Health

Weight changes after hysterectomy: recovery, appetite and menopause

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Weight can change after a hysterectomy, but the operation is not a weight-loss treatment and there is no amount that everyone should expect to gain. Understanding what was removed, why you needed surgery and how recovery is going helps put the change in context.

Start with what your operation involved

A hysterectomy removes the uterus. It may be recommended for conditions such as troublesome fibroids, persistent heavy bleeding or certain cancers, and in selected circumstances as part of treatment for endometriosis. The reason for surgery and the other treatments you need are important when interpreting changes in weight.

Removing the uterus is not a weight-loss procedure. It ends the ability to carry a pregnancy and usually ends menstrual bleeding, but it does not by itself describe what happens to your ovaries. Ask whether one or both ovaries were retained, and whether your cervix, tubes or other tissue were removed.

These are separate details even when they are discussed under one operation name. Someone recovering from uncomplicated surgery for fibroids may have a different experience from someone having cancer surgery followed by further treatment. Your discharge summary can help you keep those details clear.

An early change on the scales is not the whole story

You may notice that your weight goes up or down around the operation. Removed tissue, changes in food intake, bowel habits and the fluid changes surrounding surgery can all affect the number. That number cannot tell you, on its own, how much body fat or muscle you have gained or lost.

A large uterus containing fibroids also differs from a small uterus, so there is no standard amount that everyone should expect to lose when it is removed. Equally, a swollen or uncomfortable abdomen during recovery is not automatically a sign of lasting weight gain.

If you and your team are monitoring weight, record a trend alongside appetite, hydration, bowel function and symptoms. Avoid treating a single measurement as a verdict on your recovery. A sudden change accompanied by feeling unwell deserves attention rather than an attempt to correct it with a restrictive diet.

Nausea and reduced appetite can make eating difficult

Anaesthesia, pain, medicines and disruption to your normal routine can make food less appealing shortly after surgery. Some people feel sick or eat smaller amounts than usual. This can contribute to temporary weight loss, so it is too absolute to say that weight changes can never relate to the operation.

Tell the team if nausea or pain is preventing you from eating. They can review the likely cause and your medicines, and help you find a more manageable approach. Do not simply stop prescribed treatment or assume that persistent vomiting is a normal part of healing.

Small, manageable meals may be easier than trying to force a large plate of food. Keep track of whether you can drink, pass urine and gradually return to eating. Ongoing inability to keep fluids down, worsening abdominal pain or marked weakness needs prompt medical advice.

Cancer and its treatment need a separate nutrition plan

A hysterectomy may be one part of care for a gynaecological cancer. Depending on the diagnosis, treatment can also involve chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Changes in appetite, taste, nausea or other treatment effects can make eating and maintaining weight harder.

Weight loss in this setting should not automatically be attributed to removal of the uterus. Cancer, treatment effects and other illnesses can each contribute. Some cancer treatments are also associated with weight gain, so there is no single expected direction of change.

Report an unplanned trend to the oncology team rather than waiting until food becomes very difficult. A dietitian can help adjust meals and address nutritional needs alongside symptom treatment. The aim is to support strength and treatment tolerance, not to follow a general dieting programme while the cause remains unclear.

What the often-quoted weight study actually found

A 2009 prospective study followed premenopausal women having hysterectomy with at least one ovary retained and compared them with women who did not have the operation. It did not study an exclusively postmenopausal group, as some summaries suggest.

Over the following year, about twenty-three percent of the hysterectomy group and fifteen percent of the comparison group gained more than ten pounds. The groups differed in some characteristics before surgery, and this was an observational study. It cannot show that hysterectomy alone caused every weight change.

Those findings support paying attention to recovery and longer-term health, not predicting that every patient will gain a fixed amount. They also do not prove that preserving the ovaries prevents all weight change or that removing them guarantees it. Your own history, symptoms and pattern over time matter more than applying the group average to yourself.

Ovaries and menopause are part of the discussion

If both ovaries are removed before natural menopause, the change in ovarian hormone production is abrupt: this is surgical menopause. It is different from the gradual transition that would otherwise occur over time. Keeping one or both ovaries does not automatically produce immediate menopause, although menopause may occur earlier.

Hot flushes, disturbed sleep, vaginal dryness, changes in mood or sexual comfort can affect how you feel during recovery. Do not assume that every new symptom is caused by weight or that every weight change is explained by hormones.

Ask your clinician about symptom support and whether hormone treatment is appropriate for your circumstances. A cancer history, other health conditions and the details of surgery may affect that discussion. There is no universal promise that a particular treatment will prevent weight gain, and no fixed number of kilograms that everyone should expect.

Eat to support healing before focusing on dieting

Try to return to a varied pattern of meals with sources of protein, whole grains, vegetables and fruit, adapted to what you can tolerate. The purpose during recovery is to provide adequate nutrition and support healing. Severe restriction can make that harder, particularly when your appetite is already poor.

Convenient food can help when cooking is tiring: ask someone to prepare meals, portion leftovers or do the shopping. If a particular food worsens nausea, discuss alternatives instead of cutting out broad groups without a plan. Your existing diabetes, kidney, bowel or allergy advice still matters.

Once recovery is established, a longer-term weight goal can be discussed if it is useful to you. That conversation should take account of muscle strength, energy, food access and your relationship with eating. It need not start with a rigid target simply because you have had surgery.

Build activity gradually and check specific exercises

The source suggests gentle options such as walking, swimming, water aerobics, yoga and tai chi. They are not interchangeable immediately after an operation. Walking can usually begin gently and build up, while other activities may involve stretching, lifting, abdominal strain or immersion of healing wounds.

Follow your surgical team’s advice on swimming, including wound healing and when bleeding or discharge has stopped. Check yoga positions, water classes and other exercise before resuming them; a class labelled gentle can still be demanding. Instructions differ with the surgical route, complications and how you are recovering.

Relief from heavy bleeding or pain may eventually make movement easier, but hysterectomy is not a guaranteed cure for every cause of pelvic pain or endometriosis. Increase activity in manageable steps. Trying to make up for several weeks of recovery with sudden intense exercise is unlikely to help you judge what your body can comfortably do.

Other physical and emotional changes also deserve care

Incisions may feel tender, itchy or locally numb as they heal, but the pattern should be discussed if it is worsening or worrying you. Redness that spreads, increasing pain or new discharge is different from a steadily improving wound. New or progressive leg numbness or weakness should not simply be dismissed as an expected effect of hysterectomy.

Emotionally, some people feel relief after years of symptoms; others feel grief about fertility, worry about cancer or discomfort with changes to their body. Mixed feelings are possible. They do not mean that you made the wrong decision or that you should recover on someone else’s timetable.

Tell a trusted clinician if sadness, anxiety or sleep difficulties are persisting or affecting daily life. Support can include practical help, counselling or treatment for specific symptoms. Your recovery is broader than the number on the scales.

When to seek advice instead of watching your weight

Contact your team about continuing unexplained weight loss, a substantial unexpected change or difficulty meeting your food and fluid needs. Include when the change started, which medicines you take and whether you have pain, fever, bowel symptoms or ongoing nausea. Do not assume that surgery either explains everything or can have no connection.

After surgery, worsening abdominal pain with fever or vomiting, a concerning wound or heavy or foul-smelling bleeding needs prompt assessment. A painful swollen leg also needs urgent care. Chest pain, difficulty breathing or coughing up blood requires emergency help because a blood clot is one possible cause.

At follow-up, ask what recovery milestones are realistic for your operation and when to review nutrition, activity and menopausal symptoms. A plan based on your circumstances is more useful than a promise of guaranteed weight loss or an assumption that weight gain cannot be avoided.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

A hysterectomy and removal of the ovaries are separate surgical decisions.

The frequently quoted 2009 weight study involved premenopausal participants.

Nutrition and graded activity should support healing before restrictive weight goals.

How BeMama can help

Bring your discharge summary and a brief record of appetite, symptoms and weight changes to follow-up so the discussion starts with your actual recovery.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for chest pain, breathing difficulty or coughing up blood after surgery. Worsening abdominal pain, fever, persistent vomiting or a painful swollen leg also needs urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The scales do not distinguish tissue, fluid, muscle and body fat.
  • Persistent appetite or weight changes deserve assessment.
  • Surgical menopause depends on removal of both ovaries before natural menopause.
  • Return to specific activities according to your surgical plan.
  • Emotional recovery deserves attention too.

Frequently asked questions

Is hysterectomy a weight-loss operation?

No. It treats a medical condition, and weight changes vary with the operation, recovery and other treatment.

Can nausea after surgery affect my weight?

Yes. Reduced intake can contribute, but persistent vomiting or inability to drink needs medical advice.

Did the 2009 study involve only postmenopausal women?

No. It followed premenopausal women with at least one ovary retained.

Will everyone gain the same amount?

No. Group findings do not predict a fixed weight change for an individual.

Does removing the uterus always cause immediate menopause?

No. Immediate surgical menopause occurs when both ovaries are removed before natural menopause.

Should I start a strict diet during recovery?

Prioritize adequate nutrition for healing and discuss a longer-term plan once your recovery needs are clear.

Can I swim as soon as I feel stronger?

Check the surgical advice first, including wound healing and cessation of bleeding or discharge.

Are all yoga classes gentle enough after surgery?

No. Some positions strain healing tissues, so check what is appropriate for your operation.

Is new leg numbness automatically normal?

No. New or worsening numbness or weakness deserves assessment rather than being assumed to be routine recovery.

Can cancer treatment also change weight?

Yes. Cancer and its treatment can alter appetite and nutritional needs; involve the oncology team.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
